The system researches complex topics and produces thoroughly cited outputs. Your team built a Claude Code capability called `audit-source-coverage`. Its documentation instructs Claude to scan project prompts, review output templates, and identify missing citation validation before the coordinator is modified. When users run it, extensive search logs and discarded ideas accumulate in the active session, and subsequent publication tasks lose focus and coherence. What modification should you implement in the capability setup?

options.text: Relocate audit instructions to the main configuration file and execute `/compact` when the audit completes.
Trigger `/fork` for the audit operation so it receives the entire current conversation context.
Enable `disable-model-invocation: true` and retain the audit as part of the main conversation thread.
Set `context: fork` in the capability documentation and structure the audit as a self-contained task.

explanation: Using `context: fork` in the capability documentation isolates the audit work in a separate context, preventing exploratory notes and rejected ideas from polluting the main conversation and degrading subsequent publication tasks. Option A requires manual cleanup steps; option B inherits unnecessary context; option C disables the audit entirely rather than isolating it.

question: Your organization is using Claude Code to enhance development productivity with code synthesis, refactoring, debugging, and technical documentation. You are standardizing how Claude integrates with your workflow through custom commands, configuration files, and execution strategy decisions. Your development team is introducing SDK-driven subagents for peer review and documentation generation. They need Claude to intelligently route requests to the appropriate subagent based on task type, and they require the documentation subagent to access files without permission to modify or execute them. Which approach should they implement?

options.text: Create an agents configuration object indexed by subagent category, define each with description and instructions, and restrict the documentation subagent to a read-only tools allowlist.
Write separate subagent files containing instructions only, use file names as routing keys, and depend on parent-level permissions for tool restrictions.
Set global read-only tools in allowedTools, add routing logic to the configuration file, and skip per-subagent tool customization.
Configure agents using display names, embed the subagent role inside the instructions, and use top-level disallowedTools to prevent editing operations.

explanation: A programmatic agents map with per-subagent configuration allows explicit routing logic and granular tool permissions, enabling the documentation subagent to have a precise read-only toolset. Option B lacks routing intelligence; option C applies global restrictions that don't differentiate subagent capabilities; option D mixes configuration concerns and doesn't provide clear routing.

question: You are developing a support resolution system using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent processes complex requests including merchandise returns, payment issues, and account management. It integrates with internal services through custom MCP tools (retrieve_customer_data, find_order_details, process_refund, hand_off_to_specialist). You aim for 80%+ resolution on first contact while appropriately escalating unresolvable cases. Your organization maintains refund and escalation rules in version control and schedules Claude Code reviews only during designated review windows. A reviewer posts `@claude review once`, changes are committed, and then a second `@claude review once` generates duplicate feedback on previously flagged items. The team wants subsequent manual reviews to maintain reviewer credibility while still catching any unaddressed issues from the initial review. What should they implement?

options.text: Leave review settings as-is and have team leads manually resolve duplicate comment threads after each review cycle.
Trigger the review from the GitHub Checks interface to force Claude Code to regenerate comments against the updated code.
Switch to `@claude review` without the `once` modifier so the PR automatically receives reviews whenever code is pushed.
Create a `REVIEW.md` file with instructions to leverage earlier findings during subsequent reviews and report only new or still-pending issues.

explanation: A `REVIEW.md` file with explicit guidance on tracking prior findings enables Claude to intelligently distinguish new issues from resolved ones, avoiding duplicate comments while preserving credibility and catching genuinely unresolved problems. Option A requires manual cleanup; option B doesn't address the duplication root cause; option C enables automatic reviews that may not align with the team's scheduled review policy.

question: You are developing a multi-tier support system using the Claude Agent SDK where specialized workers handle identity verification, transaction lookups, warranty claims, and human handoff decisions. Your metrics show 75% first-contact resolution is your goal, and you need to escalate appropriately. Monitoring reveals that every request passes through all four worker agents in sequence, causing delays on simple identity checks and introducing irrelevant warranty information into basic account queries. Which architectural change would best optimize performance while maintaining specialized expertise for complex cases?

options.text: Execute all worker agents in parallel, then consolidate their outputs and have a final review step filter out unrelated findings.
Equip each worker with access to all backend capabilities and allow them to self-determine whether their expertise applies.
Implement a triage layer that evaluates the incoming request, selectively activates only relevant workers, and provides each with a focused scope.
Consolidate all worker responsibilities into a single comprehensive system prompt covering identity, transactions, warranties, and escalation logic.

explanation: A triage or coordinator layer (option C) solves the latency and irrelevance problems by invoking only necessary subagents with tailored context, avoiding wasted computation and context pollution. Option A still runs all agents and relies on post-hoc filtering, which wastes resources. Option B creates coordination overhead and unclear responsibility boundaries. Option D loses the benefits of specialized, focused reasoning that modular agents provide.

question: Your team uses Claude Code to automatically generate API specifications and migration guides from codebase changes. Reviewers have limited capacity to verify outputs, and pilot data shows that generated type signatures are typically accurate while deprecation notices are frequently incorrect. You need to focus human review effort on outputs where it will have the most impact on quality. Which approach best allocates review resources based on field-level reliability?

options.text: Calculate overall accuracy across all fields, set a target threshold, and uniformly sample remaining outputs for spot checks.
Assume outputs with clean completion signals indicate high confidence, skip review for those, and only review responses with truncation or errors.
Generate per-field confidence scores in structured output, train thresholds using labeled pilot data, and direct low-confidence fields to reviewers.
Assign a single confidence score to the entire output, review documents below a threshold, and publish all fields within approved documents.

explanation: Per-field confidence routing (option C) directly targets the observed variation in accuracy across different output types, allowing reviewers to focus on deprecation notices while trusting type signatures. Option A ignores the field-level variation that the pilot revealed. Option B conflates completion signals with correctness, which are independent. Option D treats all fields equally despite the known differences in their reliability.

question: You are building a research automation system with the Claude Agent SDK comprising a coordinator, a web researcher, a document analyzer, a findings integrator, and a report generator. During testing, the integrator agent consistently overlooks well-documented findings that appear in the middle of the aggregated evidence bundle, while reliably capturing findings from the beginning and end. How can you address this positional bias while keeping the synthesis grounded in the original sources?

options.text: Move all citations to a separate reference section and consolidate the evidence narrative into a single unbroken block.
Reorder the evidence by completion timestamp, then instruct the integrator to extract main themes from the complete bundle.
Replace detailed findings with progressively condensed summaries and pass only the most recent summary to the integrator.
Insert a structured index of key findings before the evidence bundle, then organize supporting details by explicit source and topic labels.

explanation: A structured index (option D) counteracts recency and primacy bias by making all findings equally salient at the start, and explicit organization ensures the integrator can systematically locate and reference evidence. Option A separates findings from their sources, reducing grounding. Option B does not address the positional bias. Option C loses detail and creates a lossy summarization chain that drifts from original evidence.

question: Your support team wants to create a Claude Code workflow invoked via /investigate-ticket that produces detailed analysis, runs independently from the main chat, grants Claude persistent access to project files without repeated authorization, and displays the ticket ID as a prompt when engineers run the command. What is the correct configuration?

options.text: Create .claude/skills/investigate-ticket/SKILL.md with context: fork, allowed-tools including Read and Grep, and argument-hint: [ticket-id].
Create .claude/skills/investigate-ticket.md with context: fork, allowed-tools including Read and Grep, and argument-hint: [ticket-id].
Create .claude/skills/investigate-ticket/SKILL.md with context: main, allowed-tools including Read and Grep, and argument-hint: [ticket-id].
Create .claude/skills/investigate-ticket/SKILL.md with context: fork, allowed-tools as a restrictive blocklist, and argument-hint as a validation function.

explanation: Option A correctly specifies the directory structure (SKILL.md inside a skill folder), uses fork context for isolation from the main conversation, enables persistent file access through allowed-tools, and captures the ticket ID as a hint. Option B uses an incorrect file path. Option C uses main context, which keeps the workflow in the conversation thread. Option D mischaracterizes allowed-tools and argument-hint.

question: Your CI/CD pipeline uses Claude Code to perform automated code reviews and approve pull requests. A compliance audit identifies a critical gap: the system occasionally approves changes before a mandatory test-result artifact has been verified as present and passing. This rule is absolute and cannot be bypassed. Which mechanism should you implement to enforce this constraint?

options.text: Implement a PreToolUse hook that blocks approval tool invocations if the required passing artifact is not already available.
Implement a PostToolUse hook that validates the artifact status after approval tool calls have executed.
Implement a UserPromptSubmit hook that injects artifact-verification instructions into approval requests.
Strengthen the system prompt to instruct Claude to always check for and validate passing artifacts before issuing approvals.

explanation: A PreToolUse hook (option A) prevents the approval tool from executing in the first place if the artifact check fails, enforcing the rule before any action occurs. Option B checks after approval, which is too late. Option C relies on instruction-following, which can fail under edge cases. Option D uses a system prompt, which is not a reliable enforcement mechanism for hard compliance requirements.

question: You are developing a multi-agent orchestration system using the Claude Agent SDK where a primary agent coordinates specialized sub-agents for different tasks: one retrieves information from databases, one processes images, one performs calculations, and one formats outputs. The system handles complex workflows and produces detailed, sourced deliverables. During testing, the calculation phase has access to two client tools: `process_numerical_data` for structured datasets and `process_numerical_data_advanced` for complex statistical computations. The model frequently invokes the advanced tool on simple arithmetic and the basic tool on sophisticated analyses. Both tool descriptions are nearly identical, describing only that the tool processes numbers and returns results. The team must maintain separate basic and advanced processors for different output schemas and compliance tracking. What single change would most substantially decrease incorrect tool selections?

options.text: Keep tool names as-is, add more in-prompt demonstrations to the calculation prompt, and request that Claude carefully evaluate which processor to use.
Consolidate the processors into a single unified tool, accept both simple and complex inputs, and handle input complexity internally within the tool.
Set `tool_choice` to lock the advanced processor first, then permit Claude to invoke the basic processor only if the first call yields incomplete results.
Rename tools to reflect their computational scope, rewrite descriptions to clarify appropriate use cases and limitations, and update the orchestrator to reference the new names.

explanation: Clear, distinctive tool naming combined with detailed descriptions that specify when each tool should and should not be used provides Claude with the semantic information needed to make correct routing decisions. Merely adding examples or merging tools loses the ability to track separate output contracts and audit logs. Tool choice locking is inflexible and doesn't address the root cause—Claude's inability to distinguish between the tools based on their descriptions.

question: You are embedding Claude Code into your development pipeline to automate code quality checks, generate test suites, and provide review comments on code submissions. Your prompts are designed to deliver specific, actionable feedback while reducing incorrect flagging. After several months of operation, the system marks most structured review findings with high confidence and generates test recommendations with strong certainty. Human review capacity is being scaled back, yet the team still needs to track actual defect rates in production and identify uncommon failure patterns in critical areas such as database migrations, cryptographic operations, and framework-specific idioms. Which evaluation strategy best aligns with these objectives?

options.text: Stratify high-confidence findings by change category, affected module, programming language, and finding type, then separately label actual errors and emerging patterns.
Increase the confidence threshold for accepting findings before integration, then stop human review for submissions that exceed the revised threshold.
Randomly sample high-confidence findings from across all projects, then calculate a single unified error rate for the entire review pipeline.
Focus sampling on low-confidence findings in the review queue, then assume that high-confidence approved submissions contain no defects.

explanation: Stratified sampling by relevant dimensions (change type, component, language, finding category) enables detection of rare failure modes and patterns that may be hidden in aggregate statistics, while separate labeling of errors versus novel patterns supports both defect measurement and process improvement. Uniform sampling obscures important variation, increasing thresholds without measurement is risky, and assuming high-confidence findings are error-free prevents discovery of systematic gaps.

question: You are leveraging Claude Code to boost development velocity. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and technical documentation. You integrate it into your workflow using custom commands, CLAUDE.md files, and manage the choice between plan mode and direct execution. Your team runs an automated job that parses technical specifications and pull request narratives into structured JSON requirements. Reviewers have capacity to inspect only 15% of records. The current job accepts all responses with stop_reason: end_turn and loads them directly into the database, but manual spot-checks reveal quality issues when source documents contradict each other or a field relies on loose inference. What modification would best strengthen the review workflow?

options.text: Extend the JSON schema to include per-field confidence scores, ambiguity flags, source contradictions, and supporting excerpts, then prioritize flagged records in the review queue.
Use end_turn as approval, re-invoke with higher max_tokens for incomplete outputs, then queue refusals and parsing errors for manual review.
Request logprobs and top_logprobs via the OpenAI API layer, then prioritize records with lower probability scores in the reviewer queue.
Enable source citations in the output alongside the JSON schema, then prioritize records that lack citation blocks for reviewer inspection.

explanation: Adding explicit confidence, ambiguity, contradiction, and evidence fields to the output schema gives reviewers direct signals about which records warrant scrutiny, enabling efficient prioritization of the limited review capacity. This approach is more reliable than relying on stop_reason signals, logprob inspection, or citation presence, all of which are indirect proxies for output quality and do not capture the specific semantic issues that manual review found.

question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You integrate it into your workflow using custom commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and manage plan mode versus direct execution. Your /audit command generates feedback on pull requests across four dimensions: functionality, security, performance, and maintainability. Evaluation shows that security findings are typically accepted by developers, but maintainability suggestions are often dismissed as subjective preferences. Developers are now disregarding the entire audit report, including the security findings. What action should you prioritize?

options.text: Measure precision and recall for each dimension, then refine or disable the problematic maintainability rules using examples of accepted and rejected feedback.
Increase the severity level of all findings, then instruct Claude to apply stricter judgment across all four audit dimensions.
Monitor only the aggregate acceptance rate across all findings, then update the prompt when the combined metric falls below your target.
Reorder the report to display security findings first, then mark them as critical items that require developer acknowledgment.

explanation: Measuring precision and recall by dimension identifies which specific rules are generating noise, allowing targeted refinement of just the problematic maintainability criteria while preserving effective security checks. This surgical approach restores developer trust in the entire report. Blanket severity increases, aggregate-only metrics, and reordering do not address the root cause—that maintainability rules lack sufficient specificity or relevance—and risk further alienating developers from legitimate security feedback.

question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK where a primary agent coordinates specialized sub-agents: one gathers data from public sources, one reviews academic papers, one consolidates insights, and one produces final reports. The system delivers comprehensive, sourced analyses. During evaluation, generated reports cite sources but sometimes conflate findings from a peer-reviewed publication, a commercial white paper, and an internal assessment as equivalent support for the same conclusion. The data-gathering and paper-review sub-agents currently return brief insight summaries along with a general source list. What modification best enables reliable synthesis downstream?

options.text: Have the coordinator preserve complete sub-agent logs and instruct the synthesis agent to reconstruct evidence provenance from earlier exchanges.
Add a post-processing step that enriches the final report with an expanded narrative section and a detailed references appendix.
Require each sub-agent to return structured records for each claim, including source location, publication date, evidence snippet, and study design details.
Grant each sub-agent broader tool access so it can review all available sources comprehensively before producing its summary.

explanation: Structured claim records with explicit metadata (source location, publication date, evidence excerpt, methodology) give the synthesis agent the granular information needed to differentiate between peer-reviewed studies, vendor reports, and internal surveys, enabling appropriate weighting and attribution. Relying on full transcripts requires post-hoc inference and is error-prone, post-processing enrichment happens too late to affect synthesis decisions, and broader tool access does not solve the problem of comparing evidence quality.

question: Your team uses Claude Code to manage a multi-stage content pipeline: writers draft articles, editors refine them, and compliance reviewers check for regulatory language. The /compliance-check workflow flags content for revision, but reviewers report inconsistent results: some sensitive terms are flagged while identical phrasing elsewhere passes, certain regulatory requirements are sometimes missed, and context-dependent warnings appear randomly. Which approach would most reliably reduce these inconsistencies?

options.text: Implement role-based access controls so only compliance experts can invoke the workflow.
Add a PostToolUse hook that logs all flagged terms for later audit trails.
Enable plan mode to have Claude preview its compliance strategy before processing content.
Include five concrete compliance examples—both passing and failing cases with detailed annotations—in a dedicated examples block.

explanation: Option D is correct because in-context examples, especially with edge cases and clear labeling, directly teach the model consistent decision-making patterns. Examples anchor the model's behavior to concrete scenarios, reducing variance. Option A addresses access but not consistency. Option B adds logging without improving the model's decision logic. Option C (plan mode) helps with strategy visibility but doesn't provide the specific behavioral guidance that examples deliver for consistent rule application.

question: Your team deploys Claude Code as part of an automated security audit workflow in your CI/CD pipeline. The job analyzes code changes for vulnerabilities and generates remediation suggestions. During scheduled nightly runs, the workflow starts executing but hangs indefinitely because Claude Code is waiting for developer input to clarify ambiguous findings, yet no human is monitoring the terminal. Which solution best resolves this blocking behavior?

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md directive instructing Claude Code to suppress all clarification prompts during automated execution.
Execute Claude Code in plan mode and configure the CI job to auto-approve all generated plans.
Define a custom slash command in .claude/commands/ and call it from the CI job with pre-defined parameters.
Invoke Claude Code with the -p or --print flag and supply the audit prompt as non-interactive input.

explanation: Option D is correct because the -p/--print flag with non-interactive input prevents Claude Code from entering interactive mode, eliminating the timeout. Option A relies on configuration that may not fully suppress all prompts. Option B adds approval overhead that defeats automation. Option C creates a custom command but doesn't address the underlying interactivity issue. Only the -p flag with non-interactive input guarantees unattended execution.

question: Your organization is building an internal developer platform where Claude Code supports everyday engineering tasks (ticket tracking, log analysis, deployment status checks) alongside a specialized on-call workflow that combines incident severity rules, custom escalation policies, and integration with your monitoring systems. Which architecture best achieves separation of concerns, code reuse, and team-specific extensibility?

options.text: Deploy a standard MCP server for common engineering operations, and build a separate custom MCP server dedicated to on-call logic.
Document all ticket and monitoring APIs in CLAUDE.md and use slash commands to execute shell scripts for system updates.
Create dedicated slash commands for each individual operation and rely on Claude Code's reasoning to select appropriate API calls.
Develop a single custom MCP server that handles both everyday engineering tasks and the specialized on-call workflow.

explanation: Option A is correct because it separates concerns cleanly: a maintained standard MCP server handles common, stable operations while a custom server isolates domain-specific on-call logic. This approach maximizes reuse of the standard server, maintains clear boundaries, and allows independent evolution of on-call rules. Option B mixes documentation and shell scripting, reducing maintainability. Option C creates operational overhead with many slash commands. Option D combines disparate concerns in one server, reducing reusability and making on-call logic harder to evolve independently.

question: Your organization runs an automated code quality system that performs peer review analysis, generates unit tests, and updates pull request metadata in a single Claude invocation. During testing, you observe that the review phase sometimes calls test-generation tools for stylistic feedback that shouldn't be tested, while returning unstructured prose instead of the required JSON report format. Your pipeline depends on consistent, properly formatted output. What change best ensures reliable tool usage while maintaining automated test generation capability?

options.text: Decompose into separate steps with distinct tool sets per step, restrict the review step to only its required tools, and enforce the review reporting tool using tool_choice.
Retain a single step, enhance tool descriptions, and set tool_choice to any to maximize model flexibility.
Keep one unified step, organize tools by category in names, and use tool_choice on auto for adaptive behavior.
Expose all tools to both phases, disable tool use during review with tool_choice: none, and extract JSON from text responses.

explanation: Option A is correct because separating steps with role-specific tool exposure prevents cross-phase tool misuse, and tool_choice enforcement ensures the review step always produces the required structured output. This design aligns tool availability with task intent. Option B keeps problematic tool mixing and adds description overhead without solving the core issue. Option C relies on naming conventions without restricting access. Option D disables tools entirely during review, breaking the workflow. Only separation with enforcement delivers both reliability and capability.

question: Your customer service agent, built with the Agent SDK, resolves disputes through MCP tools: retrieve_customer_profile, search_transaction_history, process_refund, and route_to_specialist. You aim for 80%+ first-contact resolution with appropriate escalation. During a dispute investigation, Claude requests both retrieve_customer_profile and search_transaction_history in one turn. The profile retrieval succeeds, but the transaction search times out sporadically. Current workarounds either mask the timeout by returning empty results or terminate the entire conversation. How should you handle this partial failure to maintain agent resilience?

options.text: Return results from both calls, mark search_transaction_history with is_error: true, and allow Claude to continue reasoning with the partial data.
Return results from both calls, discard the successful profile data after the transaction search fails, and terminate the support session.
Return results from both calls, substitute an empty transaction list for the failed search, and treat it as a successful lookup.
Return only the successful profile call, skip the failed transaction search entirely, and prompt Claude to retry the search manually.

explanation: Option A is correct because it preserves successful data, signals the error state transparently with is_error: true, and allows Claude to make informed decisions with partial context—exactly what resilient agents need. This approach maintains first-contact resolution potential despite transient failures. Option B discards working data unnecessarily. Option C masks the error, leading to silent failures and poor decisions. Option D omits the error signal and creates manual retry overhead. Only transparent error flagging with partial context enables robust agent behavior.

question: You are implementing a multi-stage content moderation pipeline for an AI-powered knowledge base using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent manages specialized review subagents: one checks factual accuracy, one evaluates tone and clarity, one identifies potential harms, and one validates source citations. The system processes user-submitted articles and publishes approved content. The team recently added a prompt-based filter that flags "potentially misleading technical terminology" to catch jargon misuse. However, this filter is triggering frequently on legitimately precise technical language that domain experts have vetted, while other filters like "unsupported inference" and "citation mismatch" work reliably. The review team is now routinely bypassing the entire moderation output. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Enforce strict output formatting with XML tags, validate structural compliance, and use format validation as the primary quality indicator.
Leave the problematic filter active, add a disclaimer about expected false positives, and instruct reviewers to manually ignore those specific flags.

Deactivate the problematic filter in the current deployment, maintain the well-performing filters, and develop a refined version using targeted examples, clearer definitions, and precision/recall benchmarks.
Turn off all moderation filters for the next release cycle, collect no automated checks, and reintroduce all filters after rewriting the entire prompt.

explanation: Option C is correct because it addresses the root cause—a noisy classifier—by removing it from production while preserving working components and investing in systematic improvement through evaluation. Option A confuses format validation with semantic correctness. Option B perpetuates the problem by normalizing false positives instead of fixing them. Option D is wasteful, eliminating useful signals alongside the problematic one.

question: You are developing a data enrichment system using the Claude Agent SDK where a primary agent coordinates with specialized subagents for data retrieval, validation, and consolidation. One subagent calls a custom tool to fetch records from a legacy database. When records cannot be retrieved—whether due to connection timeouts, invalid schema versions, missing permissions, or genuinely empty result sets—the tool returns a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and always sends the same generic message: "Request could not be completed." The coordinator agent then struggles to decide whether to retry, skip the record, or request manual intervention. How should the team redesign the tool response to enable smarter recovery?

options.text: Transform all database failures into empty result arrays so the consolidation subagent can proceed without interruption.
Enhance the tool description in the prompt so Claude learns to avoid calling tools that might encounter errors.
Add coordinator logic to automatically retry every failed database call a fixed number of times before moving forward.
Structure tool_result errors to include error classification, retry feasibility, the original query parameters, and recommended next steps.

explanation: Option D is correct because rich error information enables the agent to make context-aware decisions: transient errors warrant retries, permission issues need escalation, and empty results permit continuation. Option A hides the failure signal, making debugging impossible. Option B doesn't solve the underlying problem of ambiguous errors. Option C applies a one-size-fits-all retry strategy that may waste time on permanent failures or miss recoverable ones.

question: You are building a research synthesis platform using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent manages subagents for literature search, evidence extraction, argument mapping, and report generation. After completing an initial comprehensive literature review and producing a baseline synthesis, your team wants to explore two alternative interpretation frameworks applied to the same collected evidence without modifying the original baseline session. Each framework exploration should maintain independent conversation histories. What approach should the team implement?

options.text: Enable session snapshots for the baseline, then use snapshot restoration to branch each framework exploration while preserving the original session.
Use the SDK branch feature to fork the baseline session for each framework, then track and manage the resulting distinct session identifiers.
Continue the baseline session separately for each framework, then use distinct prompt instructions to differentiate the exploration paths. The safer, easier way to help you pass any IT exams.
Invoke continue on each framework worker, then allow the SDK to automatically select the most recent session from the working directory.

explanation: Option B is correct because the SDK's fork functionality is explicitly designed for this use case: it creates independent session branches from a baseline, preserving the original while enabling parallel explorations with separate histories. Option A uses snapshots, which are for recovery, not branching. Option C risks unintended interaction between branches and doesn't guarantee independent histories. Option D relies on implicit session selection, which is unreliable for managing multiple parallel explorations.

question: You are developing a customer issue resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK integrated with backend services via Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (retrieve_customer_profile, search_transactions, initiate_refund, route_to_specialist). The system aims for 85%+ self-service resolution with appropriate escalation. During a test session, the agent's trace shows Claude invoking search_transactions through MCP, but the transaction results never appear in the subsequent processing, and the session terminates without delivering a response to the customer. What implementation change is needed?

options.text: Pre-execute all MCP tools before agent initialization, then pass their combined outputs for Claude to synthesize in a single response turn.
Implement the agent loop so that each MCP tool call is properly dispatched, results are captured and returned to Claude, and iteration continues until a final response is generated.
Monitor the assistant's natural language output for resolution keywords, then terminate the workflow when Claude indicates the problem is solved.
Add a system prompt instructing Claude to perform all MCP backend calls directly and complete them before generating any customer-facing message.

explanation: Option B is correct because the agent loop is the mechanism that dispatches tool calls, receives results, and maintains iteration—without it, tool invocations are never processed and the session stalls. Option A eliminates the agent's ability to react dynamically to results. Option C is unreliable and doesn't address the underlying tool-result handling failure. Option D misunderstands Claude's role: it cannot execute backend operations directly; it must invoke them through the agent framework.

question: You are building a multi-agent research platform using the Claude Agent SDK where a coordinator manages subagents for source discovery, content extraction, synthesis, and publication. During quality assurance testing, published reports demonstrate strong writing and structure but occasionally contain unsupported assertions and overlook contradictions across different sections. The current workflow assigns the publication agent to self-review its draft before release. Which architectural change would most substantially enhance review effectiveness?

options.text: Assign existing subagents to review findings without sharing source excerpts, relying instead on their access to shared session context to identify inconsistencies.
Deploy dedicated reviewer agents to evaluate claim-evidence pairs for each section independently, then run a separate integration reviewer to detect cross-section conflicts and coverage shortfalls.
Have the synthesis agent consolidate all subagent contributions once, then add instructions for it to annotate unsupported statements before finalizing.
Require the publication agent to conduct an extended self-review immediately following draft completion, drawing on the full conversation history from the current session.

explanation: Option B is correct because independent reviewers with focused claim-evidence bundles avoid the cognitive bias of self-review, while a separate integration pass specifically targets cross-section contradictions that a single agent reviewing its own work would likely miss. Option A doesn't add independent scrutiny and relies on implicit context. Option C keeps the problematic self-review pattern. Option D extends self-review without addressing its fundamental limitation: an agent is biased toward its own reasoning.

question: Your team is using Claude Code to manage code quality across a microservices architecture. The system performs automated code reviews, generates integration tests, and documents deployment procedures. You need to craft prompts that deliver specific, relevant feedback and reduce noise from generic guidance. The root CLAUDE.md file has expanded to over 450 lines, covering review standards, testing frameworks, API conventions, and infrastructure checklists. Recent CI runs show that Claude Code is mixing infrastructure checklists into API design reviews and overlooking critical testing patterns. How should this team restructure the guidance to eliminate overlapping context while preserving core review standards?

options.text: Consolidate all guidance into a single CLAUDE.md file organized by section headers, then use comment markers to flag which sections apply to specific file types.
Create distinct CLAUDE.md files in each service directory and replicate the relevant testing, API, and infrastructure guidance across all locations.
Organize all guidance into separate Markdown files within .claude/rules/ without any path filtering, then depend on directory scanning to automatically load all rules.
Organize topic-specific guidance into separate Markdown files under .claude/rules/ and use paths frontmatter to restrict each rule to only the file patterns where it applies.

explanation: Option D correctly addresses the problem by separating concerns into topic-specific files with targeted path filters. This approach prevents irrelevant guidance (like infrastructure checklists) from interfering with specific reviews (like API design) while keeping all standards accessible. Options A and B either maintain the same monolithic problem or introduce duplication and maintenance overhead. Option C removes all filtering, which would recreate the original noise problem.

question: You are setting up Claude Code for automated pull-request analysis in your CI/CD environment. The system needs to query a custom HTTP MCP server that retrieves pull-request metadata and requires bearer token authentication. Your MCP configuration must be shareable across all CI runs and developer machines without committing sensitive credentials to the repository. What approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Commit a .mcp.json file that references Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in the Authorization header, and configure GITHUB_TOKEN as an environment variable in CI and developer setups.
Commit a .mcp.json file with the bearer token embedded directly in the headers, and restrict repository access to a small group of maintainers.
Store the MCP server configuration only in ~/.claude.json with the Authorization token included, and provide setup documentation for each contributor to configure manually.
Commit a .mcp.json file that references Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN in the Authorization header, and rely on Claude Code to interpolate the variable during server connection.

explanation: Option A correctly uses environment variable substitution with the standard ${VARIABLE} syntax, allowing the .mcp.json file to be committed safely while credentials are injected at runtime from CI and local environments. Option B exposes credentials in version control, which is a security risk. Option C requires manual setup and doesn't scale across teams. Option D uses incorrect syntax ($GITHUB_TOKEN instead of ${GITHUB_TOKEN}) and relies on Claude Code to perform expansion, which is not how MCP configuration resolution works.

question: Your team is developing a customer service agent using the Claude Agent SDK that handles returns, account disputes, and billing issues. The agent accesses backend systems via MCP tools (retrieve_customer_info, fetch_order_details, submit_refund, escalate_case). You are targeting 85%+ first-contact resolution with appropriate escalation. A refund operation occasionally fails when an order exceeds the return window, but the agent incorrectly reports success to the customer because the MCP response is treated as successful. How should this team properly signal tool failures to the agent?

options.text: Throw a protocol-level server exception and embed structured error information in the exception message text.
Return a standard tool result with an `error` field and expect the agent to recognize failure by analyzing the content.
Return a CallToolResult with `isError: true` set and include structured failure information in the result content.
Return a CallToolResult with `isError: false` set and include structured failure information in the result content.

explanation: Option C is correct because CallToolResult with `isError: true` is the Agent SDK's explicit mechanism for signaling tool failures, which the agent can reliably detect and act upon. Option A uses protocol-level exceptions, which are not the intended pattern for tool-level failures in the SDK. Option B relies on content inference, which is unreliable and can lead to the exact problem described (treating failures as successes). Option D sets the error flag to false, which contradicts the goal of signaling failure.

question: You are building a multi-agent research platform using the Claude Agent SDK with specialized agents for web search, document analysis, finding synthesis, and report generation. A coordinator agent orchestrates these specialists to produce comprehensive, well-cited research reports. When given a broad request like "generate a comprehensive cited report on quantum computing in finance," the coordinator must determine how to begin before assigning work to subagents. Previous executions produced polished reports but showed inconsistent topic coverage and spent resources on peripheral areas. What coordinator approach best handles this type of complex research task?

options.text: Conduct an initial discovery phase to outline the topic landscape and identify high-value research areas, then distribute prioritized subtasks that can be refined as new dependencies emerge.
Request a complete report structure from the report agent first, then assign other subagents to locate citations for each predefined section.
Launch parallel searches on the most obvious keywords immediately, then ask the synthesis agent to consolidate all findings into a final report.
Define a rigid search-to-report workflow upfront, then lock the coordinator from adjusting scope once initial subagent tasks are dispatched.

explanation: Option A is correct because it employs a discovery-first strategy that maps the problem space before committing resources, allowing dynamic refinement as dependencies and gaps are revealed. This approach prevents wasted effort on tangential areas and ensures comprehensive coverage. Option B premature commits to a structure without understanding the research landscape. Option C launches work without prioritization, risking scattered effort and incomplete coverage. Option D rigidly locks the plan, preventing the coordinator from adapting as findings reveal new priorities or dependencies.

question: Your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You have integrated custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configurations, and you understand the distinction between plan mode and direct execution. A specialized subagent handles dependency-impact analysis by inspecting affected packages before a refactor plan is approved. When a local test command intermittently times out after the subagent has already found several impacted files, the parent conversation only receives "impact analysis failed," causing the plan to lose valuable partial findings. What change best maintains system resilience while avoiding overwhelming the parent with raw exploration details?

options.text: Leave both tools and disallowedTools unset, then depend on inherited access restrictions to block further Bash attempts.
Have the parent agent directly inspect the subagent's intermediate Bash execution logs, then retry only the failed command before planning.
Have the subagent implement local retry logic for transient command failures, then return the retry attempts, partial findings, and any unresolved issues in its final result.
Move the dependency-impact analysis back into the parent conversation, then preserve all command logs for planning decisions.

explanation: Option C is correct because it enables the subagent to handle transient failures gracefully while preserving partial progress and communicating the complete status (attempts, findings, unresolved errors) to the parent in a structured summary. This maintains resilience without flooding the parent with raw logs. Option A doesn't address the timeout problem. Option B requires the parent to inspect raw logs and manually retry, which is inefficient and error-prone. Option D moves analysis back to the parent, losing the benefits of delegation and creating scalability issues.

question: Your organization is implementing Claude Code as part of a larger development platform. Engineers use it across multiple workflows including feature implementation, code review assistance, test writing, and architectural analysis. A custom slash command named /analyze is designed to help developers decide whether to request a detailed code review, create documentation, run automated tests, or proceed with implementation. During quality assurance testing, requests like "check this approach," "what could go wrong here," and "is this production-ready?" show unpredictable routing between these four paths. Team members have drafted comprehensive policy documents describing each scenario, but inconsistency persists. Which intervention would most reliably improve consistency?

options.text: Create an exhaustive decision tree that lists every possible phrase variation and its corresponding action path.
Provide 2-4 concrete examples of similar vague requests paired with the chosen action path and brief reasoning for why alternatives were not selected.
Collect a large dataset of anonymized historical interactions and allow Claude to learn the team's implicit preferences through pattern recognition.
Establish a strict rule that implementation must never proceed unless the request explicitly contains the word "implement."

explanation: Few-shot examples with explicit reasoning (option B) are more effective than exhaustive checklists for handling ambiguous cases because they teach Claude the decision-making principle rather than just listing surface patterns. Large untagged datasets (C) lack the explicit reasoning needed to disambiguate similar cases, and overly rigid lexical rules (A, D) fail on natural language variation. Concrete examples with contrastive reasoning help Claude generalize to new ambiguous requests consistently.

question: Your team is deploying a multi-step agent using the Agent SDK to handle complex customer issues spanning account recovery, subscription changes, and technical support. The agent coordinates work across specialized subagents and has access to backend tools via MCP (verify_account, retrieve_subscription, check_system_status, route_to_specialist). The system targets 75%+ autonomous resolution with appropriate escalation. During production, a worker process terminates unexpectedly while a subagent is investigating a subscription issue. When the replacement process starts, the coordinator has lost track of the verified account context, prior investigation results, and the decision to escalate if certain conditions are met. The infrastructure does not guarantee persistent local storage across restarts. Which approach best ensures safe recovery without data loss?

options.text: Enhance the system prompt with detailed memory instructions, then restart the agent from the customer's most recent message.
Attempt to locate and restore the most recent local session file, then resume execution from the last recorded checkpoint.
Use the Agent SDK's continue method to reconnect the session, then have the coordinator re-derive state from available transcript fragments.
Write application state to a durable external store before each critical decision, then load and reinject that state into the coordinator and subagent instructions on restart.

explanation: Explicit state persistence to durable external storage (option D) is the only approach that guarantees critical context—verified identity, investigation findings, and escalation decisions—survives process failures. Relying on enhanced prompts (A) or transcript reconstruction (C) risks losing verified customer data and prior decisions. Local files (B) are unreliable in distributed systems. Durable external state injection ensures both safety and deterministic recovery.

question: Your team is maintaining a large support platform built with the Agent SDK that processes customer requests for refunds, account adjustments, and service issues. The agent uses MCP-based tools to access customer records, transaction history, and approval workflows. During a post-incident review, engineers need to trace how the system decides to approve versus deny refund requests within a complex codebase spanning multiple services. Previous attempts to understand the refund decision logic involved loading entire service modules into context, which created noise and slowed analysis. What strategy should the team prioritize initially?

options.text: Run broad shell commands to search the codebase, then paste complete command output before selectively examining relevant files.
Use targeted search for refund and approval-related identifiers, then read only the matching files and trace dependencies from those entry points.
Load entire service directories into the context window, then perform a comprehensive summary before searching for refund and approval logic.
Use path-based pattern matching to identify potential files, then infer the decision flow solely from the returned file paths without reading their contents.

explanation: Targeted search followed by selective file reading (option B) minimizes context bloat while maintaining accuracy. Broad shell output (A) requires manual filtering and wastes tokens. Loading entire directories (C) creates noise before narrowing the scope. Inferring logic from paths alone (D) is unreliable and misses actual implementation details. This approach scales efficiently across large codebases.

question: Your organization is rolling out Claude Code across a monorepo containing multiple services, libraries, and applications. Testing conventions—including test file naming, assertion styles, and mocking patterns—are critical for consistency, but currently these rules are scattered across multiple local memory files in different directories. Some directories have outdated guidance, while others lack any testing documentation. This fragmentation causes Claude Code to apply inconsistent recommendations depending on which directory context is loaded. How should you consolidate these conventions to maintain consistency while keeping context efficient for non-test work?

options.text: Add a `CLAUDE.md` file to every directory containing tests and replicate the shared testing conventions in each one.
Create a project slash command in `.claude/commands/` that developers invoke before working on tests to load the conventions.
Create a `.claude/rules/testing.md` file with `paths` glob patterns targeting test files and centralize the shared testing conventions there.
Move all testing conventions into the root `CLAUDE.md` so they are loaded in every project conversation.

explanation: A centralized rules file with path globs (option C) applies conventions only to test files without bloating context for other work, and eliminates duplication and maintenance burden. Duplicating across directories (A) creates sync problems and wastes tokens. A slash command (B) requires manual invocation and is easy to forget. Loading into the root file (D) unnecessarily adds testing context to all conversations, including non-test work. Path-based rules are the scalable, maintainable solution.

question: Your team operates a customer support agent built with the Messages API that manages refund requests, billing inquiries, and account issues. The agent has access to tools including retrieve_customer_data, check_order_details, process_refund, and escalate_to_human. Company policy mandates that all refunds exceeding $750 must be reviewed by a human before execution. During testing, the agent has submitted process_refund requests for amounts above this threshold in emotionally charged billing disputes, and the application has executed these requests without human review. What measure would most reliably prevent this policy violation?

options.text: Disable tool use entirely when the customer's message contains emotionally charged language related to billing.
Implement server-side validation that rejects over-threshold process_refund requests and automatically routes those cases to escalate_to_human.
Restrict the agent to only call escalate_to_human when the conversation involves any refund request in a billing dispute.
Update the system prompt to instruct the agent that high-value refunds must always be escalated to human review.

explanation: Application-side enforcement (option B) is the only approach that guarantees policy compliance regardless of the agent's reasoning or prompt instructions. Disabling all tools (A) breaks legitimate low-value refunds. Forcing escalation on all billing disputes (C) removes the agent's ability to handle legitimate cases autonomously. System prompts (D) can be overridden by model behavior and are not a reliable enforcement mechanism. Server-side guards provide defense-in-depth protection.

question: You are developing a multi-tier information retrieval system with the Claude Agent SDK that includes separate agents for data collection, content review, metadata extraction, and final compilation. The metadata extraction agent must identify and cite the primary financial backer for each source material. In some cases, the only reference to a financial backer appears in the file's header information provided by the system, but the main document body lacks any explicit mention of funding or sponsorship. The quality assurance team flags these entries as incomplete because the extracted information lacks a verifiable text reference. How should the team address this limitation?

options.text: Designate the financial backer as a mandatory output field and execute the extraction tool again with stricter parameters before proceeding to the compilation stage.
Mark the financial backer as unverified and attach a note documenting the absence of supporting textual evidence in the document body.
Re-execute the metadata extraction agent on the same document with instructions to perform a deeper scan for any hidden funding references.
Increase the token allocation for the extraction process and reprocess the document to surface the missing sponsorship information.

explanation: When source material lacks explicit textual evidence for a data point, the appropriate response is to acknowledge the absence rather than force an extraction or retry the same operation. Option B correctly addresses this by marking the value as unverified and documenting the evidence gap, which maintains data integrity and prevents false citations. Retrying with the same inputs (C, D) or making the field required without supporting text (A) either wastes resources or produces unreliable results.

question: Your team is constructing a document processing pipeline using the Claude Agent SDK with a primary coordinator that manages workflow and delegates specialized tasks to worker agents. The document processor agent has access to three capabilities: parse_structure, extract_content, and validate_results. The coordinator must ensure that parse_structure executes first for every new document before any other operations are allowed. Which approach correctly enforces this sequential requirement?

options.text: Apply tool_choice with a value of {"type": "none"} until the coordinator explicitly provides the parsed schema.
Apply tool_choice with a value of {"type": "any"} when initiating the first document processing request.
Leave tool_choice unspecified and depend on the system's default handling of the available capabilities.
Apply tool_choice with a value of {"type": "tool", "name": "parse_structure"} when initiating the first document processing request.

explanation: The tool_choice parameter with type "tool" and a specific name forces Claude to invoke exactly that tool on the next response. Option D correctly implements the requirement to execute parse_structure first by explicitly naming it in tool_choice. Option A blocks all tools, option B allows any tool (defeating the sequential requirement), and option C provides no enforcement mechanism.

question: Your organization uses Claude Code to streamline development tasks including code generation, code improvement, troubleshooting, and technical writing. You integrate custom commands via slash notation, manage settings through CLAUDE.md, and choose between planning mode and immediate execution based on complexity. A platform team has created a custom MCP integration accessed through a /sync command that pushes updated technical specifications to a shared documentation repository. When the target branch has write restrictions enabled, the tool responds with the message "sync rejected," and Claude Code attempts the same operation multiple times before asking the developer for guidance. Which solution most effectively prevents redundant attempts while maintaining the ability to recover from transient issues?

options.text: Return MCP error responses with the error flag enabled and descriptive information that separates branch-protection errors from intermittent connectivity issues.
Configure the command to automatically retry all documentation synchronization attempts using progressive backoff intervals.
Insert a CLAUDE.md directive instructing Claude Code to abandon retries immediately when documentation synchronization encounters an error.
Return a successful response with no content when the branch is protected so the workflow can continue uninterrupted.

explanation: Claude Code's retry behavior is guided by MCP error signals. Option A correctly uses structured error responses to distinguish permanent failures (branch protection) from transient ones (temporary service issues), allowing Claude Code to retry appropriately while avoiding wasted attempts on permanent blockers. Option B forces all retries regardless of cause, option C disables all retries (preventing recovery from temporary failures), and option D masks the error, leading to silent failures.

question: Your team leverages Claude Code to enhance development velocity through code synthesis, optimization, debugging, and documentation generation. You customize behavior through slash commands, CLAUDE.md settings, and decisions about when to use exploration mode versus execution mode. After completing a comprehensive analysis of your codebase, the team wants to evaluate two different approaches to test creation based on the same initial findings. Each approach should maintain the original analysis context, keep the two investigations isolated from each other's reasoning, and ensure the original analysis remains accessible afterward. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Continue working in the most recent session twice, assigning each approach a distinct prompt identifier to separate their contexts.
Resume the original session and request that Claude organize each approach in distinct subsections of its response.
Resume the original session ID while enabling fork_session, then conduct each investigation in its own branched session.
Create two copies of the project directory and rely on the independent session histories stored within each copy.

explanation: Forking a session creates independent branches that preserve the baseline context while keeping reasoning histories separate and leaving the original session intact. Option C correctly implements this by using fork_session to branch from the baseline. Option A contaminates both investigations with each other's history, option B relies on manual organization without true isolation, and option D duplicates files rather than leveraging session management features.

question: Your organization uses Claude Code to accelerate development through code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You integrate custom commands, configure behavior via CLAUDE.md, and select between planning and direct modes based on task complexity. Your team's /analyze command categorizes pull request feedback into three buckets: implementation issues, test coverage gaps, reliability concerns, and obsolete code references. Over the past several weeks, implementation and test-coverage feedback has been consistently valuable and acted upon, but obsolete code references are frequently rejected because Claude identifies utility classes and dependency-injection handlers that are actually part of the intended design but accessed indirectly. This has caused developers to ignore the entire analysis output. Which step should be prioritized first?

options.text: Calculate precision and recall metrics for each category separately, then reduce or disable the obsolete code detection if its accuracy is too low.
Boost the priority level of implementation and test-coverage feedback so developers focus on the most reliable categories.
Consolidate all categories into a single quality metric and only adjust the prompt if the overall score declines.
Add a CLAUDE.md instruction directing Claude to apply stricter standards when identifying obsolete code patterns.

explanation: When a specific category produces noisy results that undermine trust in the entire system, the first step is to measure that category's actual performance. Option A correctly prioritizes measuring precision and recall for the problematic obsolete code detection, allowing data-driven decisions about whether to narrow or pause it. Option B doesn't address the noise, option C masks the problem with aggregation, and option D attempts a prompt fix without first confirming the root cause through measurement.

question: Your team is developing an invoice processing pipeline that uses Claude to extract line items, applies validation rules via JSON schemas, and forwards approved records to accounting software. The pipeline includes tools for extract_items, validate_invoice, approve_invoice, and flag_for_review. Monitoring reveals that when invoice totals are unclear, Claude occasionally calls approve_invoice without first successfully calling validate_invoice. This causes accounting records to be posted directly instead of being routed to the review queue. Which approach would best prevent this workflow violation?

options.text: Monitor Claude's output text for keywords like proceeding to approval and halt execution when detected.
Strengthen the system prompt with instructions to always escalate unclear totals to the review queue.
Implement a runtime check that prevents approve_invoice from executing until validate_invoice has completed successfully on that invoice.
Set tool_choice to tool for validate_invoice whenever the extraction instructions reference ambiguous line items.

explanation: An application-level gate that enforces the correct sequence of tool execution is the most reliable way to prevent workflow violations. Unlike text-pattern matching (A), which is fragile, or prompt instructions (B), which Claude may not always follow, a runtime guard ensures that approve_invoice cannot be called until validate_invoice has succeeded. The tool_choice parameter (D) does not enforce sequencing across multiple tools. This architectural control guarantees compliance with the required workflow.

question: Your team is developing a contract analysis system where Claude generates extraction rules, implements validation logic, and produces a structured output format. After deployment, edge cases involving ambiguous contract terms and calculation mismatches slip through to production testing. The current workflow has Claude review its own work in the same conversation session where it originally designed the extraction and validation approach. What modification would most strengthen the quality assurance process?

options.text: Initiate a separate Claude conversation with no prior context, then provide the business requirements, code changes, and a detailed review checklist.
Expand the generator prompt with additional contract examples and eliminate the separate review phase entirely.
Request that the same Claude session re-examine the implementation after reviewing the original design decisions.
Apply message compression in the generator session and ask it to audit the extraction rules and validation logic.

explanation: A fresh Claude session with independent context prevents confirmation bias and anchoring to the original design rationale. When Claude reviews its own work in the same conversation, it tends to reinforce its initial reasoning rather than critically challenge it. A separate session with explicit requirements and a review checklist enables objective evaluation of the extraction and validation logic. Adding examples (B) and self-review (C) do not address the fundamental bias problem, and compression (D) does not improve review quality.

question: You are implementing a multi-step research system using the Claude Agent SDK where a coordinator agent orchestrates specialized subagents for market research, competitive analysis, data aggregation, and final report generation. During testing, after the coordinator processes results from market research and competitive analysis subagents, it receives a response with stop_reason: "tool_use" that requests the data aggregation subagent. However, the current implementation treats this response as final and passes its text directly to the report generator, resulting in incomplete reports missing the aggregation phase. How should you fix the agent loop?

options.text: Create a tool_result block for the data aggregation subagent using a new tool_use_id and then proceed to report generation.
Parse the coordinator's response text for indicators like ready to aggregate and conditionally invoke the aggregation subagent.
Execute one additional coordinator iteration after sending each tool_result, then treat the following response as the report input.
Repeat the loop while stop_reason is "tool_use", send the corresponding tool_result blocks, and only treat the response as final when stop_reason is "end_turn".

explanation: The Messages API loop must continue processing whenever stop_reason is "tool_use", which indicates the model is requesting a tool invocation. Only when stop_reason is "end_turn" should the response be treated as final output. Text-pattern matching (B) is unreliable, and arbitrary iteration rules (C) do not respect the model's actual stop_reason signals. This approach ensures all requested subagents are properly executed and their results are incorporated.

question: Your team is building a customer issue resolution system using the Claude Agent SDK with MCP tools for customer lookup, order retrieval, refund processing, and human escalation. A developer is manually implementing the Messages API loop for the customer lookup tool. During integration testing, Claude requests customer lookup, the MCP server returns the customer data successfully, but Claude's next turn behaves as if the customer information was never retrieved. The application logs show the lookup was stored locally, but the subsequent Messages API call included only the original customer request and a new assistant message summarizing the lookup attempt. What should the team correct in their manual loop implementation?

options.text: Include the assistant's tool_use request in the conversation history, then add a user message containing the tool_result block with the lookup data.
Insert a user message asking for clarification before including the lookup result in the next request.
Add the lookup data as an assistant message and then instruct Claude to continue from that prefilled state.
Include the lookup data as unformatted text in a user message and resume with the original conversation.

explanation: The Messages API requires a specific conversation structure: the assistant's tool_use request must be in the history, followed by a user message containing the tool_result block. This structure allows Claude to understand that a tool was called and what data it returned. Storing the result locally without including it in the API request (as the current implementation does) breaks the conversation context. Options B, C, and D either add unnecessary steps or use incorrect message structures that prevent Claude from properly processing the tool output.

question: Your team operates a document classification system using Claude that achieves 99% schema compliance, with most documents receiving high confidence scores on extracted fields. The review capacity is limited, so only a fraction of high-confidence records can be manually inspected weekly. The team needs to measure actual error rates in production and identify emerging failure modes before they become widespread. What evaluation strategy should the team implement?

options.text: Focus reviews exclusively on low-confidence and ambiguous documents, then extrapolate accuracy for high-confidence records based on validation rules.
Rely solely on the Claude Console Evaluation Tool for monitoring and discontinue manual sampling of high-confidence records.
Select a single random sample across all high-confidence records and publish the aggregate accuracy metric each week.
Perform stratified sampling of high-confidence records by document type and critical field category, then analyze error patterns within each stratum.

explanation: Stratified sampling by document type and critical field ensures that the team detects segment-specific failure patterns and rare errors that might be hidden in aggregate statistics. This approach maintains statistical rigor while using limited review capacity efficiently. Focusing only on low-confidence records (A) misses errors in the high-confidence population. The Claude Console alone (B) cannot replace domain-specific manual review. A single random sample (C) lacks the granularity needed to identify emerging failure modes by category.

question: You are developing a multi-tier support automation system with the Claude Agent SDK where a coordinator agent delegates specialized tasks to subagents handling customer inquiries. The system includes custom MCP tools for database access and escalation management. During testing, a compliance-checking subagent frequently returns only a generic 'check failed' message, leaving the coordinator unable to determine whether to retry with different parameters, refine the scope, wait for system recovery, or accept the result as a genuine compliance gap. Reviewers also struggle to audit the reasoning behind subagent determinations. Which modification to the subagent interface would most effectively enhance system transparency and decision-making?

options.text: Return detailed subagent responses with specific error classifications, query parameters that were attempted, and any relevant compliance documentation or evidence references.
Route all compliance check failures immediately to human review before the coordinator proceeds with case synthesis.
Build retry logic within the subagent itself and report only the final determination after exhausting all internal retry attempts.
Expand the compliance database size and instruct the subagent to provide only the final check outcome without intermediate details.

explanation: Returning structured results with error classifications, attempted queries, and source metadata enables the coordinator to make intelligent decisions about retry strategies, scope adjustments, and escalation triggers, while also creating an auditable record. Generic failure messages prevent the coordinator from distinguishing between transient errors and genuine absences, making effective orchestration impossible. Immediate escalation of every failure removes the agent's ability to handle recoverable issues, while internal retries hide diagnostic information the coordinator needs. Expanding the database without improving result structure does not address the transparency problem.

question: Your team is using Claude Code to generate technical documentation through a multi-agent workflow where a primary agent coordinates research subagents that each investigate specific topics and return summaries. In a recent documentation release, the team discovered that a 2019 legacy system note and a 2024 feature update were treated as contemporaneous sources because the parent agent only received brief summaries from each research subagent without temporal context. This caused the documentation to misrepresent the currency of the information. What approach would most directly strengthen temporal accuracy when integrating findings from multiple research subagents?

options.text: Implement citation tracking for all sources and use the source URLs or publication dates to infer temporal context.
Instruct the parent agent to request detailed prose explanations from subagents whenever their summarized findings appear contradictory or misaligned.
Require each research subagent to return findings in a schema-conformant JSON format that explicitly includes publication dates and temporal justifications for every key claim.
Add a CLAUDE.md directive that instructs the parent agent to always prioritize whichever findings are labeled as most recent by the subagents.

explanation: Structured JSON responses with explicit publication dates and temporal reasoning ensure that temporal information is preserved and machine-readable throughout the multi-agent workflow, preventing the loss of critical context during summarization. Citation URLs alone may not reliably convey publication dates, especially for archived or undated content. Requesting prose recaps only addresses conflicts, not the systematic loss of temporal data in routine summaries. A CLAUDE.md directive cannot compensate for missing temporal data in the subagent responses themselves.

question: You are architecting a research platform using the Claude Agent SDK where a central coordinator distributes work to specialized subagents for web research, content analysis, synthesis, and report generation. The organization now requires the platform to incorporate bug tracking system data: retrieving issues, reading detailed ticket information, and embedding issue references in final reports. Additionally, the team has proprietary workflows that classify issue severity levels and map them to specific report sections based on internal business rules. How should you structure the tool integration to support both standard issue operations and proprietary classification logic?

options.text: Embed bug tracking instructions in the coordinator prompt and configure the web search subagent to discover issue pages through standard search queries.
Pre-export bug tracking data into structured files before each run and have the analysis subagent parse and integrate the exported data.
Develop a unified custom MCP server that consolidates all bug tracking operations and the proprietary classification workflow into a single interface.
Leverage a community-maintained MCP server for standard bug tracking operations and develop a separate focused custom MCP server for the proprietary classification logic.

explanation: Separating standard operations (handled by a maintained MCP server) from proprietary logic (handled by a focused custom server) maximizes maintainability, allows the team to benefit from community-maintained tools for standard features, and isolates custom business logic for easier iteration and testing. A monolithic custom MCP server duplicates standard functionality and increases maintenance burden. Prompt-based instructions and pre-exported files lack the dynamic, real-time access and structured interaction that MCP provides. This separation of concerns aligns with best practices for tool composition.

question: Your team is maintaining a customer support system built with the Claude Agent SDK that provides refund processing and escalation capabilities. While updating a configuration file containing refund decision language, Claude Code has already loaded the file and an `Edit` operation fails because the exact string to be replaced appears multiple times in different policy sections. The modification is intended for only one specific policy section, but the repeated language makes it difficult to identify a unique substring for the `Edit` command. How should the team guide Claude Code to implement this change reliably?

options.text: Attempt the `Edit` command again with a shorter `old_string` parameter so Claude Code can match the intended occurrence more precisely.
